lede: A rich lawyer's son, schooled at Harrow and Cambridge, who gave up his comforts to follow Gandhi, spent nearly nine years in British prisons writing world history for his daughter, and at midnight on 14 August 1947 told India it had kept its 'tryst with destiny'.

ps: Jawaharlal Nehru was born in Allahabad, today's Prayagraj, on 14 November 1889. His father, Motilal Nehru, was one of the wealthiest lawyers in India and a leader of the Indian National Congress.

Inspired by Mahatma Gandhi, he became a leader of the independence movement and was jailed nine times by the British. He was the first prime minister of independent India, from August 1947 until his death.

He built India as a secular, democratic republic, set it on a path of planned industry and science, and led the non-aligned nations in the Cold War. The defeat by China in 1962 darkened his last years. He died in New Delhi on 27 May 1964.
The family were Kashmiri Pandits, Brahmins who had moved down to the plains generations earlier. He was an only son, raised in a large house called Anand Bhavan, with English governesses and tutors.

At fifteen he was sent to Harrow School in England, then to Trinity College, Cambridge, where he studied natural sciences, and to the Inner Temple in London to train as a barrister. He came home in 1912, a somewhat bored young lawyer.
In 1916 he married Kamala Kaul. Their only child, Indira, was born in 1917. He had first met Gandhi in December 1916, at the Congress meeting in Lucknow.

1919 to 1921: the Amritsar massacre, when British-led troops fired on an unarmed crowd in April 1919 and killed hundreds, turned him against British rule. He joined Gandhi's non-cooperation campaign, gave up his practice and was first jailed in December 1921.
1927: a visit to Europe and to Moscow left him a convinced socialist, though never a communist.

December 1929: as president of Congress at Lahore he moved the resolution for Purna Swaraj, complete independence. At midnight on 31 December he raised the flag of independence on the banks of the river Ravi.
1930s: in and out of prison, he wrote letters to Indira about the whole history of the world, later published as Glimpses of World History. Kamala died of tuberculosis in Switzerland in 1936.
August 1942: when Congress launched the Quit India movement, the whole leadership was arrested. Nehru spent nearly three years in Ahmednagar Fort, where he wrote The Discovery of India.

14 to 15 August 1947: at midnight, in the Constituent Assembly in Delhi, he spoke of India awakening 'to life and freedom'. Independence came with the partition of British India into India and Pakistan. In the violence that followed, perhaps up to a million people were killed and over ten million fled their homes.
30 January 1948: Gandhi was shot dead by a Hindu nationalist. That evening Nehru told the nation on the radio: 'The light has gone out of our lives.'

1950 to 1952: India's constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, and the first general election, with about 170 million voters, most of them unable to read, was held over the winter of 1951 to 1952. Congress won and he was confirmed in office.

1954 to 1961: he signed the Panchsheel agreement with China on Tibet, based on five principles of peaceful coexistence, took part in the Bandung conference of Asian and African states in 1955, and helped found the Non-Aligned Movement at Belgrade in 1961.

October to November 1962: after years of border disputes and India's welcome to the fleeing Dalai Lama in 1959, China attacked across the Himalayan frontier. The Indian army was badly beaten. Nehru never fully recovered from the shock, and died eighteen months later.
Letters from a Father to His Daughter (1929), simple letters to ten-year-old Indira about the earth, early peoples and how history began.
Glimpses of World History (1934), nearly 200 letters from prison telling world history from an Asian point of view.
An Autobiography (1936) and The Discovery of India (1946), a long reflection on India's past written in prison, which tried to show India as one civilisation of many faiths.

As prime minister he set up Five-Year Plans, steel works and great dams, which he called 'the temples of modern India', and the first Indian Institutes of Technology. The Hindu Code Bills of the 1950s gave Hindu women rights to divorce and to inherit.
Mohandas Gandhi (1869 to 1948), his mentor, who named him his political heir, though they often disagreed about modern industry and religion in politics.
Motilal Nehru (1861 to 1931), his father, who gave up his luxurious life to join the movement too.
Vallabhbhai Patel (1875 to 1950), deputy prime minister and home minister, who brought more than 500 princely states into India. The two men were rivals and partners.
Indira Gandhi (1917 to 1984), his daughter and hostess, who became prime minister in 1966.
Rabindranath Tagore (1861 to 1941), the poet, whom he admired and whose school at Santiniketan Indira briefly attended.
Edwina Mountbatten (1901 to 1960), wife of the last viceroy, with whom he had a close friendship and correspondence from 1947 until her death.
He came to power as the British Empire was ending and the Cold War was beginning. He refused to join either the American or the Soviet bloc, and took Indian aid and arms from both.

Many of the problems he faced came from partition: millions of refugees, war with Pakistan over Kashmir in 1947 to 1948, and deep Hindu-Muslim distrust. He insisted that India would not be a Hindu state but a secular one for all its citizens.
India has remained a democracy with regular elections ever since, which few new nations of his time managed. Many historians give him much of the credit for that.
His economic planning built heavy industry and universities but was later blamed for slow growth and red tape, and was largely undone after 1991. His China policy is still debated.

His birthday, 14 November, is celebrated as Children's Day in India, and children still call him Chacha Nehru, Uncle Nehru. His daughter, grandson and descendants led Congress for most of the following decades.

myths.c: Nehru turned down a permanent seat for India on the UN Security Council.
myths.t: In 1950 and in 1955 American and Soviet figures sounded India out about taking China's seat or a new one. Nehru said India should not take a seat that belonged to China, which he wanted admitted to the UN. Whether these were ever real offers, given that changing the Council needs all permanent members to agree, is argued over by historians.

myths.c: Gandhi forced Nehru on India instead of Patel.
myths.t: In 1946, when the next Congress president was expected to lead the interim government, most of the party's provincial committees nominated Patel. Gandhi made his preference for Nehru clear, and Patel withdrew. Patel, though, was older and in poorer health, and stayed loyal as deputy until his death in 1950.

myths.c: Nehru and Edwina Mountbatten were lovers.
myths.t: Their letters show deep affection, and they met often. Her daughter Pamela Hicks has written that the relationship was loving but, she believed, not physical. No one outside the two of them can know.

myths.c: The Kashmir dispute was Nehru's fault alone.
myths.t: He took the case to the United Nations in 1948 and offered a vote of Kashmir's people that never took place, which critics say was a mistake. But the dispute also grew from partition itself, the late decision of the Maharaja, the 1947 invasion from Pakistan, Cold War politics and choices by many later leaders.

myths.c: Nehru chose his own birthday as Children's Day.
myths.t: During his lifetime India marked Children's Day on 20 November, in line with the United Nations' Universal Children's Day. It was moved to his birthday, 14 November, only after his death in 1964, in his memory.
